summary: Defines lightweight versions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, the protocols hosts use to join multicast groups, that simplify the full versions. It also considers how they interoperate with the full and older versions. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let a device say which senders it wants to hear from in a multicast group. This RFC defines smaller versions of both that drop the rarely used way of naming senders to avoid, so routers and switches do less work.

questions: how does lw-igmpv3 differ from igmpv3
subtitle: A stripped-down subset of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 that drops the filter mode almost nobody uses.

tldr.problem: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let a host name the exact sources it wants from a multicast group. The cost is a filter mode with two settings, extra report record types and router state that changes often.
tldr.mechanism: The lightweight versions drop the EXCLUDE filter mode with a named source, keep only four report record types, and let the router keep one group timer and a list of source timers instead of a filter mode.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from February 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. The message formats are unchanged, so lightweight and full implementations can sit on the same network.

today: RFC 5790 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The lightweight protocols it defines are subsets of IGMPv3 and MLDv2 and do not change their message formats, so they can be used alongside the full versions on the same network.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IGMP version 3, defined in RFC 3376, and MLD version 2, defined in RFC 3810, add source filtering that the earlier versions IGMPv1, IGMPv2 and MLDv1 do not have. A host running IGMPv3 or MLDv2 can tell its upstream router which group it wants to join by saying which sources it does or does not intend to receive multicast traffic from. In the other direction, a multicast router can learn which sources are of interest, and which are not, for a particular multicast address, and uses that information when forwarding multicast data packets.

That source filtering is built on two filter modes. If a host wants to receive from specific sources it sends a report with the filter mode set to INCLUDE. If it does not want to receive from some sources it sends a report with the filter mode set to EXCLUDE. A source list for the given sources is included in the Report message. A multicast router also uses the two filter modes when it processes those reports: it manages the requested group and source addresses and keeps group timers and source timers to maintain the forwarding state of the desired groups and sources under a given filter mode.

Those factors correlate with each other, so the rules become relatively complex, and the interface states could be changed frequently. The RFC's argument for simplifying is practical: applications do not often use EXCLUDE mode to block sources, because a user or application usually wants to specify the desired source addresses rather than the undesired ones. Even when a user explicitly refuses traffic from some sources in a group, other users on the same shared network may want those sources, and the traffic is forwarded to the network anyway. Blocking sources is generally unnecessary.

This RFC therefore proposes simplified versions of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, called Lightweight IGMPv3 and Lightweight MLDv2, or LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2. They are subsets of the standard versions. They support both Any-Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast communication without a filtering function that blocks sources, and the operations performed by hosts and routers, including switches that perform IGMPv3 or MLDv2 snooping, are simplified. Because the lightweight versions are fully compatible with the full ones, a host or router that has implemented the full version needs no change to cooperate with lightweight hosts or routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast is one-to-many delivery: the sender sends once and every receiver gets the copy. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let a receiver say which senders it wants. This RFC keeps that ability but removes the part almost nobody uses, which is naming senders to refuse.

sections.title: The Four Ways to Join a Group
sections.content:
The RFC defines four join operations, and the difference between them is which senders the receiver ends up accepting.

A (*,G) join is triggered by a host that wants to join a group G. The host receives from all sources sending to group G. This is typical of Any-Source Multicast communication. An (S,G) join is triggered by a host that wants to join a group G and specifies a desired source S. The host receives traffic only from source S sending to group G.

An INCLUDE (S,G) join is the same as an (S,G) join: the host joins group G under INCLUDE filter mode and names source S as desired. An EXCLUDE (*,G) join is the same as a (*,G) join: the host joins group G under EXCLUDE filter mode. An EXCLUDE (S,G) join is a host joining group G under EXCLUDE filter mode while naming source S as undesired. This last operation is not supported by LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2.

In short, the lightweight protocols keep both ways of naming a sender you want, and both ways of joining without naming anyone, but drop the single way of naming a sender you do not want.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver can ask for a group in two ways: take traffic from anyone sending to that group, or take traffic only from one named sender. The lightweight protocols allow both, and drop the third option of naming a sender to avoid.

sections.title: The Simplification Method
sections.content:
The stated principle is to simplify the host's and the router's behavior as much as possible to improve efficiency, while guaranteeing interoperability with the full versions and introducing no side effects on applications. For convenience the RFC discusses IGMPv3, since MLDv2 inherits the same source filtering mechanism, but it also gives MLDv2's unique specifications where they differ.

Group members. LW-IGMPv3 inherits the service interface model of IGMPv3, which is the call IPMulticastListen(socket, interface, multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). In the lightweight protocol, INCLUDE mode on the host side has the same use as the full version for an INCLUDE (S,G) join, while EXCLUDE mode is preserved only for excluding null source lists. A null source list denotes a (*,G) join, as used by IGMPv2, IGMPv1 and MLDv1. The one operation that disappears is the EXCLUDE (S,G) join.

Multicast routers. In IGMPv3 the router filter mode optimizes the state description of a group membership. As a rule, once a member report is in EXCLUDE mode the router filter mode for the group is set to EXCLUDE, and when all systems stop sending EXCLUDE mode reports the filter mode may move back to INCLUDE. The group timer identifies that transition.

In LW-IGMPv3, hosts primarily send INCLUDE requests and can also request an EXCLUDE (*,G) join, which the router can interpret as a request to include all sources. Without the more general form of EXCLUDE requests, the router no longer needs to maintain the EXCLUDE filter mode, and its state model reduces to a multicast address, a group timer and a set of source records. The group timer is kept to represent a (*,G) join: when the router receives a (*,G) join it sets its group timer and keeps the source list for sources named in previously received source records, and when the group timer expires the router may change to receiving the listed sources only. The definition of a source record is the same as in the full version.
sections.plainLanguage: The router no longer has to remember whether a group is in one of two modes. It keeps a timer for the group as a whole and a timer per sender, and that is enough to decide what to forward.

sections.title: What Group Members Send
sections.content:
LW-IGMPv3 uses the same two sets of messages as the full version, Query and Report. There is no difference in the definition or use of the Query message. The report types are reduced, because the operation that triggers an EXCLUDE (S,G) join is omitted.

Full IGMPv3 defines three group record types. The Current-State Record is denoted by MODE_IS_INCLUDE, referred to as IS_IN, or MODE_IS_EXCLUDE, referred to as IS_EX. The Filter-Mode-Change Record is denoted by CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE, referred to as TO_IN, or CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE, referred to as TO_EX. The Source-List-Change Record is denoted by ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES, referred to as ALLOW, or BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES, referred to as BLOCK. LW-IGMPv3 inherits the actions on a change of interface state and on the reception of a query, but the IS_IN and IS_EX record types are eliminated and Current-State Records are replaced by other records.

Change of interface state. When the state of an interface of a group member host changes, a State-Change Report for that interface is transmitted immediately from that interface. The type and contents of the group records in that report are worked out by comparing the filter mode and source list for the affected multicast address before and after the change. The requirements for the computation are the same as for the full version, but the rules are simpler because there are fewer message types. Moving from INCLUDE with source list A to INCLUDE with source list B sends ALLOW(B-A) and BLOCK(A-B). Moving from INCLUDE with source list A to EXCLUDE with an empty source list sends TO_EX({}), and so does moving from INCLUDE with an empty source list to EXCLUDE with an empty source list. Moving from EXCLUDE with an empty source list to INCLUDE with source list B sends TO_IN(B).

To cover the possibility of the State-Change Report being missed by one or more multicast routers, it is retransmitted the Robustness Variable minus one more times, at intervals chosen at random from the range zero to the Unsolicited Report Interval.

Reception of a query. As in the full version, a lightweight host does not answer a query immediately. It delays its response by a random amount of time bounded by the Max Resp Time derived from the Max Resp Code in the received Query message. The host may receive a variety of queries on different interfaces and of different kinds, such as General Queries, Group-Specific Queries and Group-and-Source-Specific Queries, each of which may require its own delayed response. Before scheduling a response the host must consider previously scheduled pending responses and in many cases schedule a combined response, so it must maintain a timer per interface for scheduling responses to General Queries, a per-group and interface timer for scheduling responses to Group-Specific and Group-and-Source-Specific Queries, and a per-group and interface list of sources to be reported in the response to a Group-and-Source-Specific Query.

Record types. The table below shows how the full and lightweight versions line up. The letter x stands for a non-empty source address list and ({}) stands for an empty one. The lightweight protocols do not use EXCLUDE filter mode with a non-empty source list, so the operations that would need it are marked as not applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: A host still sends the same two kinds of message: a query comes from the router and a report goes back. What changes is that the host now only uses four kinds of record inside a report, and the rules for working out which one to send are shorter.

sections.title: What Multicast Routers Keep
sections.content:
The major difference between the full and the lightweight protocols on the router side is that in the lightweight version the filter mode is discarded and the function of the group timer is redefined. The states a lightweight router maintains are reduced and the protocol operation is greatly simplified.

Timers. In both the lightweight and the full IGMPv3 routers a source timer is kept for each source record and is updated when the source appears in a received report. It indicates the validity of the source and has to be consulted when the router takes its forwarding decision. The group timer, which in the full IGMPv3 is used for moving the router's filter mode from EXCLUDE to INCLUDE, is redefined in the lightweight protocols to identify the non-source-specific receiving state maintained for a (*,G) join. Once a group record of TO_EX({}) is received, the group timer is set to represent this (*,G) group join. When the group timer expires, there are no more listeners on the attached network for this (*,G) group. If at that moment there are unexpired sources, meaning source timers greater than zero, the router changes to receiving traffic for those sources only.

There is one difference from the full version in how the timers interact. In the full version, if a source timer expires while the router filter mode is EXCLUDE, its source record is not deleted until the group timer expires, because the record is needed to indicate undesired sources. In the lightweight version there is no need to keep such records for blocking specific sources, so an expired source timer means the source record is deleted immediately, without waiting for the group timer to time out.

Forwarding rules. A full version multicast router consults IGMPv3 state information when it decides whether to forward a datagram from a source, based on the router filter mode and the source timer. In LW-IGMPv3, because there is no filter mode, the group timer and the source timer are enough. The table below lists the suggestion the lightweight protocol gives to the routing protocols.

Receiving records. When the router receives Current-State Records it resets its group or source timers and updates its source list within the group. In the source-specific group reception state, where the group timer is zero and a source timer is greater than zero, the source list holds the sources whose traffic the router will forward. In the non-source-specific group reception state, where the group timer is greater than zero, the source list remembers the valid sources to receive traffic from after the router moves to source-specific reception.

Although the lightweight host only sends a subset of the messages of the full version, the lightweight router should be able to process as many messages as possible so that it stays compatible with a full version host. If the report type is IS_EX(x) with a non-empty source list, the router treats it as the same type of report with an empty source list. When the router receives an IS_IN report it appends the reported source addresses to the previous source list, with their source timers set to the Group Membership Interval. On receiving an IS_EX({}) report, the router sets the non-source-specific receiving state by resetting the group timer value and keeps the previous source list unmodified.

On receiving Source-List-Change and Filter-Mode-Change Records the router resets its group and source timers, updates its source list within the group, or triggers group queries. The queries are sent for the sources that are requested to be no longer forwarded to the group. If the report type is TO_EX(x) with a non-empty source list the router treats it as the same type with an empty source list. An ALLOW(B) report appends B to the source list and sets the source timers to the Group Membership Interval. A BLOCK(B) report leaves the source list unchanged and sends a group query for the sources in A*B, the sources that were in the list and are now being blocked. A TO_IN(B) report appends B to the source list, sets the source timers to the Group Membership Interval and sends a group query for A-B. When the group timer is greater than zero it also sends a general group query. A TO_EX({}) report leaves the source list unchanged and sets the group timer to the Group Membership Interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps two kinds of timer. One runs for the whole group and means there are still listeners who want traffic from anyone. One runs per sender and means that sender is still wanted. When the group timer runs out, the router forwards only from the senders whose own timers are still running.

sections.title: Working with Other Versions
sections.content:
Lightweight hosts and routers must interoperate with hosts and routers running the full versions, and must interoperate gracefully with hosts and routers running IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or MLDv1. The lightweight protocols make no change to the message formats of the group Query and Report messages that the full versions use.

Hosts. A lightweight host's compatibility mode is held in the Host Compatibility Mode variable, which can be IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or IGMPv3. When a lightweight host behaves on its interface as LW-IGMPv3, the Host Compatibility Mode of that interface is set to IGMPv3 and the host sends a subset of the IGMPv3 Report messages, which a multicast router running the full or the lightweight protocol on the same LAN can recognize. The Host Compatibility Mode of an interface is set to IGMPv2, and its IGMPv2 Querier Present timer is set to the Older Version Querier Present Timeout seconds, whenever an IGMPv2 General Query is received on that interface. It is set to IGMPv1 in the same way when an IGMPv1 Membership Query is received.

In the presence of older version group members, a lightweight host may allow its Report message to be suppressed by an IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 membership report. Because transmitting IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 packets reduces the capability of the lightweight system, and this can act as a protection mechanism, the choice to enable or disable backward compatibility may be configurable.

Routers. A lightweight router does not process IS_EX(x) and TO_EX(x) reports directly. When it receives them from full version hosts it must translate them internally to IS_EX({}) and TO_EX({}) respectively and behave accordingly. A lightweight router placed on a network where some routers have not been upgraded to IGMPv3 behaves exactly as a full IGMPv3 router does in that situation.

A full IGMPv3 router keeps a Group Compatibility Mode per group record, whose value is IGMPv1, IGMPv2 or IGMPv3, to indicate which version of the IGMP protocol applies to that group. The value is set according to the version of the received reports. When the Group Compatibility Mode is IGMPv3, the lightweight router performs the lightweight protocol for that group. When it is IGMPv2, the router translates an IGMPv2 Report to TO_EX({}) and an IGMPv2 Leave to TO_IN({}). When it is IGMPv1, it translates an IGMPv1 Report and an IGMPv2 Report to TO_EX({}). For MLDv1 the method is the same, and an MLDv1 Report translates to TO_EX({}) and an MLDv1 Done to TO_IN({}).
sections.plainLanguage: The message formats do not change, so a lightweight device and a full device can talk to each other and to the same router. Where an older version sends a message the lightweight protocol does not have, the router rewrites it into the equivalent lightweight record.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The lightweight protocols require no additional procedure for the implementation of the related protocols or systems, such as IGMP and MLD snooping, the multicast routing protocol, and the operation of application sockets, while the processing load on the switches and routers that run IGMPv3 or MLDv2 snooping and the multicast routing protocols may be greatly decreased.

For Source-Specific Multicast, the lightweight protocol follows the same rules as RFC 4604 except for the change of message types due to the simplification. A lightweight host should not invoke a (*,G) join, that is TO_EX({}), or a (*,G) leave, that is TO_IN({}), for applications whose multicast addresses are in the SSM address range. An upstream lightweight router must not establish forwarding state on receiving them and may log an error.

For the Multicast Source Filter APIs, which are defined in RFC 3678, a lightweight IGMPv3 host should implement either the IPv4 Basic MSF API or the Protocol-Independent Basic MSF API, and a lightweight MLDv2 host should implement the Protocol-Independent Basic MSF API. The IPv4 Advanced MSF API and the Protocol-Independent Advanced MSF API are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing else in a switch or router has to change to run this. The rule that matters for applications is that a host should not ask for a whole group by name when the address is in the source-specific range, because the upstream router will refuse to set up forwarding state for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the security considerations are the same as those of the full version of IGMPv3 and MLDv2, and adds nothing of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds no security rules. What applies is what already applied to the full IGMPv3 and MLDv2 protocols.
